subject: physics

items.q: Two devices are connected across the same 12 V supply. Device X draws a current of 2.0 A and device Y draws a current of 0.50 A. Which statement about the two devices is correct?
items.correct: Device X has the greater power, so it transfers more energy each second.
items.misconception: Device X has the greater power, so it transfers more energy overall.
items.why: The two words are used interchangeably in everyday speech, as in 'the power used last month'. Power is a rate. Divide the energy transferred by the time in seconds to compare powers fairly.
items.random_wrong: Device Y has the greater power, because it draws the smaller current.

items.q: A potential difference of 12 V drives a current of 0.25 A through a circuit device. What is the power transfer in the device?
items.why: When the operation is not recalled, adding the two given numbers feels safe because it uses both of them. Adding a pd in volts to a current in amperes adds unlike quantities. The equation multiplies them, and the product is in watts.
items.random_wrong: 9 W

items.q: In the equation P = V I, what does each symbol stand for and in which unit is it measured?
items.correct: P is power in W, V is pd in V and I is current in A.
items.misconception: P is power in W, V is the pd in A and I is the current in V.
items.why: Both quantities describe 'how strong' the electricity is, and the letter V is used for both the quantity and the unit. Potential difference is measured in volts by a voltmeter across a component; current is measured in amperes by an ammeter in series.
items.random_wrong: P is power in W, V is pd in ohms and I is current in A.

items.q: A current of 0.60 A flows through a resistor of resistance 12 ohms. What is the power transferred in the resistor?
items.why: In (current)^2 x resistance the bracket is read as enclosing everything that follows it. The bracket in (current)^2 encloses the current alone. The resistance is never squared.

items.q: The current through a fixed resistor is doubled. What happens to the power transferred in the resistor?
items.correct: The power becomes four times greater, because P = I^2 R squares the current.
items.misconception: The power becomes two times greater, as current and power are proportional.
items.why: Direct proportion is the familiar pattern, and the square is treated as decoration rather than as part of the arithmetic. Substitute: (2I)^2 R = 4 I^2 R. Doubling a squared quantity multiplies the result by four.
items.random_wrong: The power is unchanged, because the resistance itself has not altered.

items.q: Which line gives the units the specification uses for power and for potential difference?
items.correct: Power is measured in watts, W, and pd is measured in volts, V.
items.misconception: Power is measured in joules, J, and the pd is measured in volts, V.
items.why: Watts appear on appliances in contexts where students are asked about 'energy use', so the two ideas merge. One watt is one joule per second. A watt is a rate, so it always needs a time before it becomes an energy.
items.random_wrong: Power is measured in watts, W, and pd is measured in amperes.

items.q: Which line gives the units the specification uses for current and for resistance?
items.correct: Current is measured in amperes, A, and resistance in ohms.
items.misconception: Current is measured in amperes, A, and resistance in volts, V.
items.why: V = I R links all three quantities, and students remember the equation rather than which unit belongs to which symbol. Match each symbol to its unit: R to ohms, V to volts, I to amperes, P to watts.
items.random_wrong: Current is measured in coulombs, C, and resistance in ohms.

items.q: An electric kettle is plugged into the mains and switched on. Which statement best describes why the kettle is built as it is?
items.correct: It is designed to bring about a particular energy transfer.
items.misconception: It is designed to create new energy from the mains supply that it uses.
items.why: Words such as 'generating' and 'producing power' are everyday usage, and appliances appear to make heat from nothing. Energy is only ever transferred between stores. Track where the energy came from as well as where it ends up.
items.random_wrong: It is designed to store the electrical energy the mains delivers.

items.q: A 2000 W kettle is switched on for 2 minutes. A 100 W lamp is switched on for 1 hour. Which transfers more energy?
items.correct: The lamp, because energy transferred depends on the time as well as the power.
items.misconception: The kettle, because it has the higher power rating of the two appliances.
items.why: The two words are used interchangeably in everyday speech, as in 'the power used last month'. Power is a rate. Divide the energy transferred by the time in seconds to compare powers fairly.
items.random_wrong: The kettle, because its rating already gives the energy it transfers.

items.q: A hairdryer has a power of 1500 W. It is switched on for 4 minutes. How much energy does it transfer?
items.why: The number in the question is used exactly as written, and the unit line for t is not checked. In E = P t the time must be in seconds. Convert minutes or hours to seconds before substituting.

items.q: A food mixer is plugged into a wall socket and switched on. How is energy transferred while it is in use?
items.correct: Electrically from the ac mains to the kinetic energy of the motor.
items.misconception: Electrically from the ac mains to the thermal store of the mixer motor.
items.why: All appliances warm up, and heating is the transfer students meet first, so it is offered for every device. Identify what the appliance is designed to do. A mixer is designed to turn a blade, so the useful transfer is to kinetic energy.
items.random_wrong: Electrically from batteries to the kinetic energy of the motor.

items.q: A cordless drill and an electric kettle are both in use. Which statement about their supplies is correct?
items.correct: The drill is supplied by batteries and the kettle by the ac mains.
items.misconception: The drill is supplied by the ac mains and the kettle by its batteries.
items.why: The abbreviations ac and dc are easily swapped, and 'straight from the wall' suggests dc for the mains. Batteries give a direct current, always in one direction. The mains supply is an alternating current.
items.random_wrong: Both are supplied by the ac mains, as both contain a heating device.

items.q: A lamp is connected to a cell and lights up. Which statement about work in this circuit is correct?
items.correct: Work is done, because charge is flowing through the lamp.
items.misconception: No work is done, because nothing in the circuit can be seen moving.
items.why: Work is first met as force x distance with a visible object moving, so an invisible charge flow does not look like work. Work is done whenever energy is transferred by a force. The source does work pushing charge around the circuit.
items.random_wrong: Work is done, because the lamp uses up the current.

items.q: Which equation does the specification give for the energy transferred by electrical work in terms of power?
items.correct: energy transferred = power x time, with the time measured in seconds.
items.misconception: energy transferred = power / time, with the time given in seconds.
items.why: The first electrical equation students meet is V = I R, which is usually rearranged by dividing, so division becomes the default operation. Check the words: power = potential difference x current. Both a larger pd and a larger current give a larger power, so the two must multiply.
items.random_wrong: energy transferred = power x time, with time given in minutes.

items.q: A kettle has a power of 2000 W. It is switched on for 90 s. How much energy does it transfer?
items.why: When the operation is not recalled, adding the two given numbers feels safe because it uses both of them. Adding a pd in volts to a current in amperes adds unlike quantities. The equation multiplies them, and the product is in watts.

items.q: A lamp has a power of 60 W. It transfers 5400 J of energy. For how long was it switched on?
items.why: The first electrical equation students meet is V = I R, which is usually rearranged by dividing, so division becomes the default operation. Check the words: power = potential difference x current. Both a larger pd and a larger current give a larger power, so the two must multiply.

items.q: Which line gives the equation for energy transferred in terms of charge flow, with the correct units?
items.correct: E = Q V, where Q is charge flow in coulombs and V is pd in volts.
items.misconception: E = Q V, where Q is charge flow in amperes and V is the pd in volts.
items.why: Charge and current are both described loosely as 'electricity', and the ampere is the unit met first. The ampere is the unit of current, the rate of flow. The coulomb is the unit of the charge that has flowed.
items.random_wrong: E = Q / V, where Q is charge flow in coulombs and V is the pd.

items.q: A motor connected to a 12 V supply takes a current of 5.0 A for 60 s. How much energy is transferred?
items.why: Q and t are both numbers taken from the same sentence, and both are needed, so the wrong one is substituted into E = Q V. Q is the charge that has flowed, in coulombs, found from current x time. Only then does it go into E = Q V.

items.q: An electric motor transfers 5400 J of energy when the potential difference across it is 18 V. What charge flowed through it?
items.why: Dividing is the habitual move for electrical equations, carried over from rearranging V = I R. Both a larger charge flow and a larger pd transfer more energy, so the quantities must be multiplied.

items.q: Which units does the specification give for energy transferred and for time in E = P t?
items.correct: Energy in joules, J, and time in seconds, s.
items.misconception: Energy in joules, J, and time in minutes, min.
items.why: The number in the question is used exactly as written, and the unit line for t is not checked. In E = P t the time must be in seconds. Convert minutes or hours to seconds before substituting.
items.random_wrong: Energy in watts, W, and time in seconds, s.

items.q: Which units does the specification give for charge flow and for potential difference in E = Q V?
items.correct: Charge flow in coulombs, C, and pd in volts, V.
items.misconception: Charge flow in amperes, A, and the pd in volts, V.
items.why: Charge and current are both described loosely as 'electricity', and the ampere is the unit met first. The ampere is the unit of current, the rate of flow. The coulomb is the unit of the charge that has flowed.
items.random_wrong: Charge flow in coulombs, C, and pd in ohms, Ω.

items.q: A circuit device is switched on. Which statement about the power of the device is correct?
items.correct: Its power is the pd across it times the current, and the energy given each second.
items.misconception: Its power is the pd across it added to the current through it, giving watts.
items.why: When the operation is not recalled, adding the two given numbers feels safe because it uses both of them. Adding a pd in volts to a current in amperes adds unlike quantities. The equation multiplies them, and the product is in watts.
items.random_wrong: Its power is the total energy that it transfers, whatever the time taken.

items.q: Heater X transfers 30 000 J in 60 s. Heater Y transfers 48 000 J in 120 s. Which heater has the greater power?
items.correct: Heater X, because it transfers 500 J each second and Y transfers 400 J.
items.misconception: Heater Y, because it transfers more energy altogether than heater X does.
items.why: The two words are used interchangeably in everyday speech, as in 'the power used last month'. Power is a rate. Divide the energy transferred by the time in seconds to compare powers fairly.
items.random_wrong: Heater Y, because it was switched on for the longer period of time.

items.q: A cook boils the same pan of water on a 2400 W hob and then on a 900 W hob. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The 2400 W hob raises the temperature of the water faster than the 900 W hob.
items.misconception: The 2400 W hob transfers more total energy, because it has more power.
items.why: The two words are used interchangeably in everyday speech, as in 'the power used last month'. Power is a rate. Divide the energy transferred by the time in seconds to compare powers fairly.
items.random_wrong: The 900 W hob raises the temperature of the water more quickly than the 2400 W hob.

items.q: What is the National Grid?
items.correct: A system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers.
items.misconception: A system of cables alone that links all of the power stations to consumers.
items.why: The pylons and cables are the visible part of the system, while transformers are hidden inside substations. The transformers are part of the grid, and they are what make transmission over long distances efficient.
items.random_wrong: A system of power stations that generates all of the energy consumers use.

items.q: Electrical power is transferred from a power station to homes. In which order are transformers used along the way?
items.correct: Step-up transformers first, then step-down transformers near consumers.
items.misconception: Step-down transformers first, then step-up transformers near the consumers.
items.why: 'Step down' sounds like leaving the power station, and 'step up' sounds like arriving at the consumer. Follow the path: the pd is stepped up for transmission, then stepped down to a much lower value for domestic use.
items.random_wrong: Step-up transformers at both ends, to keep the pd high all the way.

items.q: Why is the National Grid an efficient way to transfer energy from power stations to consumers?
items.correct: A high pd gives a low current, so less energy is wasted heating the cables.
items.misconception: A high pd makes the energy travel along the transmission cables much faster.
items.why: Potential difference is imagined as a push that speeds the electricity up, so more pd sounds like a quicker delivery. The benefit is the reduced current, not a change of speed. Less current means less heating of the cables.
items.random_wrong: A high pd lowers the resistance of the long cables used in the National Grid.

items.q: A transmission cable of resistance 5.0 ohms carries a current of 1000 A. What power is wasted in heating the cable?
items.why: Direct proportion is the familiar pattern, and the square is treated as decoration rather than as part of the arithmetic. Substitute: (2I)^2 R = 4 I^2 R. Doubling a squared quantity multiplies the result by four.

items.q: A kettle is labelled 2000 W. How much energy does it transfer?
items.correct: The label gives the power, not the energy. Energy transferred also depends on time: E = P t, so 2000 W for 90 s transfers 180 000 J.
items.misconception: The number on the label is the energy, so a 2000 W kettle transfers 2000 J.
items.why: Power and energy are both 'how much' quantities in everyday speech, and the rating is the only number printed on the appliance. Read the watt as 'joules every second'. Multiply the power by the number of seconds to get the energy transferred.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A current of 0.60 A flows through a 12 ohm resistor. What is the power?
items.why: The equation looks like V = I R, and the small superscript 2 is easy to miss when reading quickly. Square the current first, then multiply by the resistance. Writing 0.60 x 0.60 x 12 out in full keeps the square visible.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does a current of 2 A tell you?
items.correct: Current is the rate of flow of charge, measured in amperes, A, and amp is acceptable for ampere.
items.misconception: The ampere measures the amount of electricity stored in a component, which the component then uses up.
items.why: Everyday language talks about a battery 'holding electricity', so current is imagined as a quantity that sits in the circuit. Current is a flow, not a store, and it is not used up. Two amperes means two coulombs of charge passing each second.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A 2000 W kettle and a 100 W lamp are both switched on. Which transfers more energy?
items.correct: It depends on the time as well as the power: the lamp left on for an hour transfers more than the kettle used for two minutes.
items.misconception: The appliance switched on for the longer time is the more powerful one, because I confuse how long a device runs with how powerful it is.
items.why: Power ratings are the only figures given on appliances, so they are treated as a complete answer on their own. Energy transferred = power x time. A comparison of energy needs both the power and the time for each appliance.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A current of 5.0 A flows for 60 s through a 12 V motor. How much energy is transferred?
items.misconception: E = Q V = 5.0 x 12 = 60 J, using the current in place of the charge flow.
items.why: Current and charge flow are both about moving charge, and the current is the number given in the question. Charge flow is current x time. Work out Q first, then multiply by the potential difference.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do transformers increase the energy delivered to consumers?
items.correct: No. Transformers change the potential difference; they do not create energy or increase the power transferred.
items.misconception: A step-up transformer increases the power, so more energy reaches consumers.
items.why: 'Step up' is heard as 'more of everything', and the increase in pd is assumed to increase the power too. When a transformer raises the pd it lowers the current in the same ratio, so the power transferred is not increased.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does raising the transmission pd reduce the energy wasted?
items.correct: It reduces the current, and the power wasted in the cables is I^2 R.
items.misconception: It reduces the resistance of the cables.
items.why: Both changes would reduce the waste, and resistance is the quantity in the equation that students expect to be able to control. The cables have a fixed resistance. Only the current changes, and squaring it makes the saving large.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.2.4 Energy transfers
